steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement with curly braces to import both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.seedCode:
// Import React and useState here

// Your component will go below
steps.expectedOutcome: The import statement for React and useState is added at the top of the file.
successCriteria: The code includes an import statement that imports both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState. This gives you access to React's core library and the useState hook for managing state in your component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check your import statement. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react' using the correct syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. You need to import both React and useState from the 'react' package to proceed.

steps.title: Create the main Dashboard component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named Dashboard that returns JSX. You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.hint: Define a component that returns a JSX element like a div. Remember to use TypeScript syntax.
steps.expectedOutcome: A Dashboard component is defined that returns JSX.
successCriteria: The code should contain a functional component named Dashboard that returns JSX (e.g., a div element).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the Dashboard component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the component is named exactly 'Dashboard' and returns JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Dashboard component is not properly defined. Check that you've created a functional component named Dashboard that returns JSX.

steps.title: Initialize userCount state
steps.instruction: Inside your Dashboard component, initialize a state variable called userCount using useState. Set its initial value to 0 and specify its type as number.
steps.hint: Remember to call useState<number>(0) and destructure the returned array into [userCount, setUserCount].
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a numeric state
const [count, setCount] = useState<number>(0);
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a userCount state variable initialized to 0 with type number, ready to track user count data.
successCriteria: The code should include a useState call with <number> generic and initial value 0, destructured to [userCount, setUserCount].
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the userCount state with the correct type and initial value.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using useState with the <number> type annotation and initializing it to 0.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to initialize a state variable called userCount with useState<number>(0).

steps.title: Initialize revenue state
steps.instruction: Inside the Dashboard component, initialize a state variable named 'revenue' with useState, setting its initial value to 0 and explicitly typing it as number.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook with a generic type parameter to specify the state type.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a typed state variable
const [count, setCount] = useState<number>(0);
steps.expectedOutcome: The Dashboard component will have a typed revenue state variable initialized to 0.
successCriteria: The code should include a useState call with type parameter <number> and initial value 0, assigned to a variable named 'revenue' (or destructured as [revenue, setRevenue]).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the revenue state with proper TypeScript typing.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using useState with the <number> type parameter and initializing it to 0.
steps.feedbackWrong: The revenue state initialization is missing or incorrect. Remember to use useState<number>(0) to create a typed state variable.

steps.title: Initialize isActive state
steps.instruction: Inside your Dashboard component, add a new state variable called 'isActive' using useState. Initialize it with the value 'true' and explicitly type it as boolean.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook you imported earlier. Remember to specify the type as boolean using angle brackets.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a boolean state variable
const [isActive, setIsActive] = useState<boolean>(true);
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component will have a third state variable named 'isActive' with initial value 'true' and boolean type annotation.
successCriteria: The code must include a useState call for 'isActive' with type boolean and initial value true, placed after the existing state declarations.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the isActive state variable with boolean type and initial value true.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've declared 'isActive' with useState, typed it as boolean, and set the initial value to true.
steps.feedbackWrong: The isActive state wasn't properly initialized. Check that you used useState<boolean>(true) and named the variable 'isActive'.

steps.title: Define handleUserIncrement function
steps.instruction: Inside your Dashboard component, define a function named handleUserIncrement that increments the userCount state by 1 when called.
steps.hint: Use the setUserCount function from the useState hook. You can update the state based on its previous value.
steps.expectedOutcome: A handleUserIncrement function is added to the component that will increase userCount by 1 each time it's called.
successCriteria: The code should contain a function named handleUserIncrement that uses setUserCount to increment userCount by 1.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the handleUserIncrement function that updates the userCount state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function correctly increments userCount by 1 using setUserCount.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function isn't defined correctly. Remember to create a function named handleUserIncrement that increments userCount by 1.

steps.title: Define handleRevenueUpdate function
steps.instruction: Inside your Dashboard component, define a function called handleRevenueUpdate that adds 100 to the revenue state when called.
steps.hint: Create a function that uses the revenue state setter to update the value by adding 100 to the current revenue.
steps.expectedOutcome: A handleRevenueUpdate function is defined that will update the revenue state by adding 100 when called.
successCriteria: Function named handleRevenueUpdate is defined
Function updates revenue state by adding 100
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the handleRevenueUpdate function that will update the revenue state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function is named exactly 'handleRevenueUpdate' and it adds 100 to the revenue state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleRevenueUpdate function is not properly defined. Check that you've created a function with the correct name and logic to update revenue.

steps.title: Define handleToggleActive function
steps.instruction: Define a function called handleToggleActive that toggles the isActive boolean state value. Place this function after the other handler functions in your component.
steps.hint: Create a function that calls the setter for isActive with the opposite of the current value. You can use the functional update pattern: setActive(prev => !prev).
steps.expectedOutcome: A handleToggleActive function is defined that toggles the isActive state between true and false.
successCriteria: The function should be named handleToggleActive, use the setIsActive setter, and toggle the boolean value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the handleToggleActive function that toggles the isActive state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function correctly toggles the boolean value using setIsActive.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function doesn't seem to toggle the isActive state correctly. Check that you're using setIsActive to update the state.

steps.title: Return the main dashboard container
steps.instruction: In the return statement of your Dashboard component, replace the existing <div> with a <div> that has the className 'dashboard' as the main container.
steps.hint: The className attribute in JSX is used to apply CSS classes. You need to add className='dashboard' to the opening div tag.
steps.expectedOutcome: The main container div now has the className 'dashboard', which will be used for styling.
successCriteria: The return statement should contain a <div> element with className='dashboard' wrapping the existing content.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the main dashboard container with the correct className.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added className='dashboard' to the opening div tag in the return statement.
steps.feedbackWrong: The main container div is missing the className 'dashboard'. Please check the return statement.

steps.title: Add dashboard header with status
steps.instruction: Inside the Dashboard component's return statement, add a header section below the existing <h1> that displays the current isActive status.
steps.hint: Add a <div> or <section> element with a paragraph that shows the isActive state value.
steps.expectedOutcome: The dashboard UI now shows a header section that displays whether the dashboard is active or inactive based on the isActive state.
successCriteria: Add a new JSX element (div/section) after the <h1>
Display the isActive state value in a paragraph or similar element
Use JSX curly braces {} to embed the isActive variable
Optionally format the boolean value (e.g., 'Active'/'Inactive')
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a header section that displays the current activity status. The dashboard now shows whether it's active or inactive based on the isActive state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the header section might be missing some elements. Make sure you've added a container element after the <h1> and are displaying the isActive state value using JSX curly braces.
steps.feedbackWrong: The header section with status display wasn't added correctly. Check that you've added JSX elements after the <h1> and are displaying the isActive state value in the UI.

steps.title: Add metrics section with user count and revenue
steps.instruction: Inside the return statement of your Dashboard component, add a new <section> element after the header. Inside this section, add two <div> elements: one to display the current userCount value and another to display the current revenue value.
steps.hint: You can add the section directly after the existing header element. Use curly braces {} to embed the state variables (userCount and revenue) inside the JSX.
steps.expectedOutcome: The dashboard will now display a metrics section showing the current user count and revenue values.
successCriteria: A <section> element exists in the return statement
The section contains two <div> elements
First <div> displays the userCount value using {userCount}
Second <div> displays the revenue value using {revenue}
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a metrics section that displays the current user count and revenue values.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have: 1) A <section> element, 2) Two <div> elements inside it, 3) Both state variables displayed using curly braces.
steps.feedbackWrong: The metrics section is missing or incomplete. Add a <section> element with two <div> elements that display the userCount and revenue values.

steps.title: Add control buttons with click handlers
steps.instruction: Add three buttons inside the return statement: one to increment users, one to update revenue, and one to toggle the active status. Each button should call its respective handler function when clicked.
steps.hint: Use the <button> element with onClick handlers. The handlers are already defined: handleUserIncrement, handleRevenueUpdate, and handleToggleActive.
steps.expectedOutcome: The dashboard will have three interactive buttons that update the state when clicked, enabling real-time data manipulation.
successCriteria: Three <button> elements are added
Each button has an onClick handler
onClick handlers call handleUserIncrement, handleRevenueUpdate, and handleToggleActive respectively
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the control buttons with their click handlers. The dashboard now has interactive controls to update user count, revenue, and active status.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some buttons, but not all three are present or correctly wired. Make sure you have buttons for incrementing users, updating revenue, and toggling active status, each with the correct onClick handler.
steps.feedbackWrong: The buttons are missing or not correctly connected. Add three <button> elements with onClick handlers that call the existing functions: handleUserIncrement, handleRevenueUpdate, and handleToggleActive.
